item.title: 工頭也答不出來的地方！工友知道嗎？ ft. 蘇巧慧
item.itunes:title: 工頭也答不出來的地方！工友知道嗎？ ft. 蘇巧慧
item.itunes:author: 工頭堅。旅行長
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

================================================

# 精華：你以為在日本，其實在新北

If we talk about New Taipei City, it's like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. That's one way to put it, it's a bit of a metaphor, yes, exactly. If you know of any other great spots in New Taipei City, could you share them with me? Even places that look like they're in Japan but are actually right here in New Taipei, could you share those too? I really want to know. Everyone wants to share the scenes they experience there with others, so being able to photograph these spots is really. important, I think. >> As I just mentioned, that's an abstract ideal, a wish of mine. But in plain terms, it just means you should be able to find what you want anywhere. Hello everyone, I’m your Chief Traveler, Kung Tung-chien. I mentioned last time that our channel would start hosting podcast-style conversations again, since we’ve done them before and are now bringing them back. We already had one guest for a conversation, and I believe many of you have already seen that video. Today, wow, I’m quite happy to discuss this topic because.

# 開場：新北是台北的 Bed Town？

last time, our conversation ended up revolving around the loneliness of modern people. >> Especially the loneliness of people in my generation—it got a bit sentimental toward the end. But today, I feel much happier because many of our viewers love traveling to Japan. That’s right, we’re going to talk about a topic related to traveling in Japan today. As you all know, over the last year or two—or rather, since the beginning of this year—I’ve been traveling the Tokaido in Japan. The Tokaido is the old road that ran from. Kyoto to Edo, and many people used this ancient route to reach Edo, which is today's Tokyo. But you’ll notice that not everyone lives in the heart of Tokyo; many people actually live in the surrounding prefectures. These are the so-called "bedroom towns" where people commute in the morning and return to sleep at night. As a resident of New Taipei City, I realized that where I live is a bit like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. This is our topic for today, and who better to. discuss it with than our guest? We’ve invited Legislative Yuan member Su Chiao-hui to join us today. Thank you, Kung Tung-chien. Hello to all the viewers, I am Otter Mom. >> When Otter Mom tells stories to children, she's "Otter Mom." >> Otter Mom is very well-known. >> Yes, yes, thank you everyone. >> So, Otter Mom also often takes everyone out on trips! >> Alright, as I mentioned earlier, while today's topic is travel-related, seeing you today made me think of something.

# 來賓登場與兩人的片場往事

that probably 99%of our audience doesn't know. We're usually so transparent, is there really something people don't know? >> We share a common experience. I heard that during the years you were studying law in the US, you worked part-time on film sets—first helping your husband with student productions in Texas—and you've even said that you were the best free labor back then. >> Oh, if you want to talk about that, are you asking if I worked as a production assistant? >> We started filming back in college, yeah, we've been filming since our. college days. Basically, it started with him as a student director and me behind the lens—wait, he was behind the lens, and I did everything else besides that, all the administrative work. So you could call me the co-producer. >> That's the truth. >> Right, you could call me an admin assistant, or a producer, anything really; it was just a two-person team, after all. OK, the reason I ask is because many people only know Janet from her days as a "travel expert," but folks, Janet was also in the film industry when she was younger. >> Really? Yes. >> I was doing production design back then , so that included building sets and everything. >> I think production design is just amazing. >> It's so exhausting. >> Production design is truly incredible. You see, they can create that entire scene from scratch. We had a famous saying back then: everything outside the camera frame is fake. Exactly, and later on, I saw how AI is so advanced now, right? A lot of things are done with green screens and computer-generated animation. >> Oh, but it's not the same. I felt that back then, production design could manage everything inside the frame,. from the color coordination to—and I'm very impressed by this—everything from the curtains and dining tables to the table runners. Even the creases in the table runners. Yes. >> Everything had to be perfectly aligned with the director's vision before the actors stepped in and we called "camera ." So, since you're so particular about the visuals, I have a sudden question: when you go to a place now, is your first thought whether it's a good spot to film? Yes.

# 用拍片的眼光看景點：一定要有打卡點

>> Honestly, yes. I truly believe that where we've been leaves a mark, and no experience is ever wasted. I really enjoy having studied law; I feel that my ability to analyze, break down, and synthesize logic and situations has been incredibly helpful, making me much more efficient at handling things now and easier to grasp the crux of an issue. And I feel that in this realm of filming and producing movies, I've also learned a great deal from every single role in the process, since making a. movie is a collaborative effort. For instance, whenever I see a scene now, I find myself thinking about which spot or which angle is the one I want most —if I could only take one photo. >> What is the specific shot that could capture the scene before me and turn it into a story to tell others? >> Or, what is the final image I want to leave behind from this press conference ? >> This idea of deciding what final image I want to capture in a place has almost. become a standard procedure for me, or perhaps, is it >> a kind of pursuit? >> Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. So, I feel that when I look at a scenic spot now, if I ever have the chance to, say, develop a tourism industry, I would really want to create that one specific image that stays in people's hearts. I believe that when there's an image that sticks with visitors, they'll come back a second, third, or fourth time, and bring even more people with them. >> Absolutely, and I have to add one more. point. Because nowadays, everyone has social media—whether it's Instagram, or like me, doing YouTube—everyone wants to share the image of where they are with others, so being able to photograph a spot is really important. >> What I said earlier was an abstract ideal, my wish, but in plain terms, it just means that every place needs a landmark photo spot that makes people want to come back. >> Whether it's natural or man-made, nowadays, it's all about that photo op. It's a must! Which leads us to our topic today: it's essentially a conversation between two New Taipei City residents. >> But in fact, many New Taipei residents are likely just like us; I was born in Yilan, moved to Taipei with my grandfather, and then my father moved us to New Taipei. Many New Taipei residents weren't necessarily born here , but it's precisely because of this that people from all different counties.

# 從東海道宿場談到「衛星變繁星」

and cities live here. >> Exactly. >> We finally, or I should say, we eventually came to treat this place as a—that’s wonderful. Hearing you say that makes us very happy. Yes. >> Really, really, really. Maybe people moved here at first because the housing prices over there were too high to afford, but after moving, they really started to treat this place as their home. Returning to what I mentioned earlier, I’m currently walking the Tokaido. People might still have the impression of the Tokaido as a place in period dramas where feudal lords are. carried in palanquins, but having reached the final stretch, I’ve found that what I’ve seen the most along the way are post stations. These so-called post stations were where people used to stay; after walking for a stretch, they needed a place to stop for the night, so these stations naturally formed settlements. >> Those post stations have now become satellite cities around Tokyo, gradually developing from those original settlements. When Japan began building its railways, the first line. ran from Shimbashi to Yokohama, and then it extended along what is known as the Tokaido, connecting all these post stations. If you look at this narrative , it’s actually exactly the same in Taiwan. >> Exactly the same. >> Exactly the same; our historical development is almost identical. >> Yes, and the railway line, what used to be the main thoroughfare, is now the railway line, and many people from the south traveled up along it. Now, what I want to say is... >> Around us now, it has actually developed around Taipei into... >> How many districts are there in total? 29 districts. In New Taipei City? 29 districts, yes. >> New Taipei City now has 29 districts. I think this is the desire that everyone has—to have the opportunity to be in charge, to be their own master. So when people talk about satellites, it's like revolving. around another star, right? Your speed and your state are likely more constrained by others. I think it's like this: if you look at our New Taipei, the administrative districts weren't drawn like this in the past, so we used to say "one Fu, two Lu, three Zhuang"—and Zhuang refers to Xinzhuang. >> That's the first time I've heard "three ". People nowadays might prefer hearing "three Jia", but it's actually " Xinzhuang" first. It was only after the river channel in Xinzhuang silted up. that things shifted to the deeper Mengjia area. So Xinzhuang is really the place where our ancestors first landed and pioneered, hence the name Xinzhuang. >> Right, actually the names Xinzhuang and Shinjuku are somewhat similar. Somewhat similar, yes. It started along the river, and gradually, as we settled in flatter areas, formed communities, and began farming, our clans and tribes slowly evolved. >> Take Shulin as an example, actually... >> The place where I serve, Shulin—if you just look at its place names, it’s actually very interesting. >> Really? >> Yes, but Shulin is further divided into what are now neighborhood names. >> Because of its ancient place names; I'll start by introducing a central point called Tandi. >> Right, right, so there must have been a pond there. OK, OK. >> That's where people with the surname.

# 樹林古地名與鐵道的由來

Peng started living, they lived there. >> Right. >> Raising ducks. >> And then, gradually, it reached Shanjia . " >> Under the mountain," because as we moved out of the pond area, houses started appearing at the foot of the mountain, hence Shanjia, which is around the current Shanjia Station. >> Right. >> I love hearing this. Yes, and then after you pass that and cross the mountain, it becomes a vast flat area; because they grew oranges there, it's called... >> Oh. >> So that's where it comes from. >> Because I'm really not familiar with the Shulin area. For me, I'm sharing this by using the place where I've served for ten years to show that our ancient place names really reflect the footprints left by our ancestors when they first arrived to conduct various commercial or reclamation activities, and they named them accordingly. That's how we got the current administrative districts, but these districts still. have to evolve along with our development. Ah, so when you said some people accepted the railway while others didn't, it’s not quite like that. The railways back then were built for specific purposes. In my area, Shulin, my neighborhood of Sanjia was actually a coal mining hub at the time. >> Oh, so that’s why it had a station. Exactly. They built the railway to transport coal out from the mines. It ran from Sanjia Station all the way to Shulin Station. Since our area in Ganyuan has vast flatlands that produced the best rice, it was even. classified as a special agricultural zone. Because the quality was so high, the rice had to be shipped out, which is why we have Shulin Station. That’s our origin story. The railway had to be built here because of the produce. Because the goods were here, the railway followed, which is why we developed so early on. But of course, because times have changed, these products are no longer the most essential goods today. Naturally, just. like places like Jiufen or Jinguashi, they’ve faded a bit because there are different business models now. So, how do we create new opportunities for these places so they can find their place again? Since they already have the railway infrastructure, figuring out how to work with their current conditions is the challenge for us today. >> OK, I was listening so intently just now, because I really love hearing stories like this. As you all know, I’ve been doing these historical. walking tours, mainly focused on Japan. This brings me to something I’ve been thinking about a lot these past few years. I’m a resident of New Taipei City, though most of my work is based in Taipei. Mm. >> But the thing is, when we go to Tokyo, you’ll notice that the stations surrounding Tokyo have massive passenger traffic every morning and evening. Why? Because people live right next to them. >> We do too, which is why I even built a station called Pengming Station.

>> That’s right, exactly. >> Beyond the daily commute, these surrounding areas are also where Tokyo residents go for tourism and relaxation . >> So I’ve been imagining—since I used to like comparing Japan to Taiwan in my videos, like how I once compared Kyushu to Taiwan—if we look at New Taipei City, it’s like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. New Taipei is, well, it's like three counties combined,. because New Taipei surrounds Taipei. >> It has both mountains and the sea, and I don't know if you've thought about this, if you often travel to Japan, >> Look, I always keep mine covered. It’s no wonder, your mobile phone wallpaper is a map of New Taipei City. >> Let me tell you a secret, I also used a New Taipei City map as my computer desktop background before. >> Exactly, exactly. No, I think, I think it’s about finding that sense of belonging, which is why we talked about treating this place as home earlier. Right, back to what I was saying, I’ve been making comparisons, so has. everyone noticed that around Tokyo, there’s Chiba Prefecture, Saitama Prefecture, and Kanagawa Prefecture? These are all places that many Taiwanese people love to visit. >> That's right. Take Kanagawa Prefecture for example, since it’s closer to the sea, so simply put, if there’s a comparison to be made, Tamsui could correspond to Yokohama. Some might think, shouldn’t Yokohama correspond to Keelung? No, no, no. Actually, if you look at the earliest ports of the capital, Tamsui should correspond to. Yokohama. >> And then, they have an ancient city called Kamakura, plus another train line that everyone loves to ride and take photos of—the Enoden line. What I want to discuss with you is, how should New Taipei City correspond to these Japanese prefectures and cities in the future? For instance, during your interpellation, you mentioned that the Jiufen-Jinguashi bus route has 5.92 million passengers a year, while I’ve participated in the Crown North Coast route, which only has 38,000. It’s.

clearly a wonderful place, so how can this be resolved? >> I think it’s like this—you’ve really touched upon exactly what I want to do most. >> As everyone is likely aware, I have another role as a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, so I will frankly report to everyone that my policy vision is regional balance and city identity. Regional balance is my ideal, and achieving city identity is my vision. Because there is regional. balance, everyone will identify with the city; there is actually a coherent context to this. Right, so regional balance lies in the fact that our 29 districts in New Taipei City are, in my opinion, all different. They differ in history, culture, landscape, customs, and industrial needs. >> So you must adapt to local conditions and develop according to the local situation. Therefore, we have cities, villages, mountains, and the seaside. So as a New Taipei City team, from the. leaders and grassroots civil servants to the citizens themselves, I really feel we shouldn't just think about heading into Taipei City. >> Instead, even if my job is still currently in Taipei City, >> for my weekends and my time after work, can I stay in New Taipei City to fulfill my living needs, while also letting people from Taipei, or even most other people, come to my area and fall in love with it? That is our real. ambition! What this means is going from being satellites orbiting Taipei City to becoming 29 individual stars. So, " shining bright," that is the vision for New Taipei's future: satellites becoming stars, making New Taipei shine . So, for example, why would they be willing to come here? I think the first step is to create unique features. >> That is why I proposed the New Crown Coast project. >> Yeah. >> It covers my eight coastal townships, yeah. >> It really runs from Bali, Tamsui, Sanzhi, Shimen, all the way to Gongliao. . Right. >> 28 fishing ports, 145 kilometers of coastline, right? Once you organize the fishing ports, first and foremost, you mustn't neglect the fishing industry; it still needs to run smoothly. >> Yes. >> But then you can start developing the tourism that everyone likes now, plus near-shore marine experiences, coastal activities, and even have " all-transport" tourism. Right. >> So can we use, say, since my word isn't objective enough, big data analysis or. I didn't want to cut in because that part was so well-stated. Between us, I actually once wrote a sci-fi novel—this isn't in the outline—but what I mean is... >> I imagined that in a parallel universe, our North Coast could have something like the Enoden—the Enoshima Electric Railway—a railway line stretching all. the way from Tamsui to Keelung, which would solve transportation for every location. # 鑽石山城與「新北五道」

>> And to be honest, strictly speaking, New Taipei City seems to have more mountains than ocean. Our mountain area is very large, including Pinglin, Pingxi, Shuangxi, and Wulai— these five are the mountain regions. >> It is truly beautiful. Last time, I went to walk in Pingxi myself, including the hiking trails at Xiaozi Mountain. >> That day happened to be just after it had rained the day before. >> Oh. >> And you can just imagine that green. >> That shade of green is incredible; you. can see how amazing nature is. How can there be so many different shades of green? >> It really is a magical thing. So when I talk about the mountain regions, I refer to New Taipei's "Five Paths": the hiking trail, the railway, the tea path , the mining path, and the old street. Within my mountain regions, I have the hiking trails that people already walk on. The railway and mining/tea paths— well, let's say the trails and railways are for transportation, the mining and. tea paths are historical remains, and the old streets are our current business models. Combining these five, you have different ways to explore from the past to the present, each with its own story. I think stories bring out so many charming aspects; so yes. >> It depends on how you want to play. In the past, many people called me a travel expert, so they would always ask me how domestic tourism should be developed. I certainly pride myself on having a lot of ideas, but honestly, what you just mentioned about mining. tunnels and old streets is something I hadn't really thought about before. >> I brought some photos, can I share them ? Yes, sure, let's take a look. >> Go ahead and share. >> Let me see. Look, this is our railway, our Pingxi line. >> The Pingxi line train was originally built for transporting coal, just like I mentioned with Shulin, it was for coal, which is why those train stations were opened there. Now, many of them, like Pingxi Station or even Jingtong Station, are over a hundred years old, so they actually look beautiful in photos.

# 照片導覽：從平溪、坪林到卯澳灣

>> Beyond just photos, let me jump in—if this were in Japan, it would definitely be a scene from an anime. If you posted this on X, I’m sure many Japanese friends would love it. Next. Right, perhaps because my printer today couldn't capture exactly what I saw at the time, this is at the Jingtong mining area, inside the coal mine memorial park. The whole scene, the way the trees grow, it’s so rugged and natural that you’d think it’s a place where forest spirits appear. I. find it amazing, so my dream for the future is to be able to host reading events in a place like this. Reading events? >> Yes, exactly. I think concerts, book fairs, these could all become events that develop naturally and freely in that environment. I feel that our New Taipei City has such a natural stage of mountains and seas, where we could organize all sorts of different exhibitions. I believe that as long as trails like these are better maintained , any of these things could be achieved. . Now look, this is our... >> This is Pinglin tea. >> This was shot by Abukuan. What’s it called? Yu Tea Plantation? Yes, it's in Pinglin. Maybe not this exact spot, but in Pinglin, many commercials are filmed there. Even like this one in Shiding, the Xu’s handmade vermicelli; because the water quality is so good, the texture of the noodles is uniquely chewy. In these natural landscapes, there’s actually a lot of. craftsmanship and even unique products, and like this photo, I think... >> Where is this? I really don't know this one. >> The bus stop at Baishawan—this is the check-in spot we were talking about earlier, right? >> It’s actually just a bus waiting shelter, >> but they designed it in a way that makes everyone want to take photos for social media. To be honest, at the beginning, when Commissioner Qiao asked me how long it had been since I did domestic travel in New Taipei City, I really didn't know about this place. >> Look, isn't it beautiful? Yes, and this here is the three-level bridge in Jinguashi, Ruifang. >> Because it has one level, two levels, and another one below, making it a three-story bridge. Back then, they were used for different waterways and foot traffic, so they’re all filled with stories now. This is Jinshan. It’s not just mountains; they grow sweet potatoes in the loose soil on the mountainside. But down in the flatter areas, the soil becomes fine and. clay-like, which holds water well. So, we grow sweet potatoes on the hills and lotus roots and bamboo shoots in the lowlands, before it flows into the sea. Jinshan is truly a place where the mountains meet the sea. >> This lotus pond is also very beautiful. >> This is Mao’ao in Gongliao. Oh, what are they doing here? >> They are participating in the thousand-person swim across Mao’ao. >> There’s also this activity. To be honest, I truly regret that this photo can’t even capture one ten-thousandth of the real experience. When I arrived,. I was shocked because the seawater was so clear—I felt like, "Wow, the stunning blue water I haven't seen in so long." I thought to myself, "Are there really waters like this on the main island of Taiwan?" I thought you’d have to go to Penghu or somewhere else to see this, but no, we have it right here at our own Mao’ao in Gongliao. Unfortunately, due to my schedule, I couldn't participate in the event today. The event isn't just about swimming; it’s also about snorkeling. The special thing is that if you put on a mask and dive down, you can see colorful coral reefs right below. It’s so easy, and you can see so much . It really makes you realize, "My goodness, the North Coast and the Northeast Corner have it all"—from windsurfing, kayaking, and jet skiing, all the way to beach volleyball and snorkeling. And I haven't even told you about the hot springs in Jinshan yet! I finally got to see one. >> Yes, and at night, you can even go lamp. fishing for squid. >> There really is just so much to do. Actually, as I was watching you show these photos earlier, I found myself getting a bit reflective. The reflection was because, as I mentioned just now, I have this identity as a travel expert. >> So, whenever many places want to promote their tourism, they often invite me to come and experience them. >> For instance, in Hualien and Taitung, whether it was to promote the mountains or the seaside, I've been there many times. But since my time is very limited now, what with running my YT. channel and writing books, I sometimes feel that the time cost of traveling all the way there is just too high for me. >> Oh. >> But I just realized that I don't actually have to go that far; I can find these landscapes right here in New Taipei City where I live. >> I can invite you to Jinguashi. >> Because there is a rising trend there now. >> It's called "workation." >> Oh, OK. Yeah, our old houses have been renovated into guesthouses. They prefer.

# 金瓜石居遊與淡蘭古道

guests who book by the week. You go there, and amidst the rolling mountains , there's a beautiful old house with a very modern, comfortable interior. It’s a hotel, so all services are provided, and you just focus on writing your book. >> Writing a book. So many young digital nomads go there to stay for a week or a month, and the food is also incredibly. delicious. >> This reminds me of when the pandemic started; I noticed that Japan introduced this concept called " workation." >> It means you're working there, but you're actually in a vacation spot. >> The internet is very convenient, you know. >> The point is that the internet is very accessible, everyone can go. >> As long as there's internet, you can go anywhere. And if you suddenly want to return to Taipei, it only takes an hour or so from New Taipei, right. >> I'll keep that in mind. >> Yeah, I... >> Next time I'll take you there, I'll take you next time. >> Actually, just from what you said, I already have so many images in my head, whether it's the sea or the mountains. One thing is, it's really about having those visuals. >> It needs visuals, and also, since I mentioned I live in Yilan, I later learned that my great-great-grandparents used to carry Yilan mountain produce. Exactly. >> And they would bring it to Tamsui to sell. >> So that route was previously called the Caoling Historic Trail, and now it's collectively known as the Danlan Historic Trail. >> Right, right. >> From this end, I... >> That’s right, I was talking about it with Lin Guo-zhang, as we were pushing for it on both sides, making our way all the way here from Toucheng in Yilan . In fact, the Danlan Trail is such that if you walk it once, not only is it good for exercise, but it also cleanses your spirit; plus, by experiencing all the cultural stories of the ancestors along the way, you won’t even need to memorize history textbooks anymore. >> I was previously on the pilgrimage route in the Tokaido, and people said. it was very difficult. While walking it , I thought it was beautiful, but I also realized that the Danlan Trail is just like that, it’s just not well-developed. >> Developed, that is. Yeah. >> We’ve even discovered that along the Danlan Trail, there are tons of Earth God shrines. >> In principle, there are 250 of them. >> It’s a pilgrimage route. >> Yes, so we basically want to create this "Earth God Stamp Collection Journey." >> Collect 250 stamps. >> Collect 250 Earth God stamps and we'll grant you an honorary citizenship. >> 250 is really not easy to get. >> 250 of them, yeah, exactly. Right, but this brings up how many people go to Japan to walk the Shikoku Pilgrimage. I’ve actually been thinking that Taiwan is very suitable for religious-themed travel, as Taiwan is a place where folk religion is very vibrant, with all kinds of religions, and I think the Earth God is perfect for this. When we look at Shiding, there’s actually also a Mazu pilgrimage route here, as well as a pilgrimage route for the Prince Nezha temples. Actually, in these mountainous. areas, you’ll find that in the past, everyone hoped that besides their own hard work, heaven could bless them and the gods could protect them, so they brought their faith along as they moved forward, making these paths very meaningful to walk. >> Alright, so privately, I’m asking for one more theme: the Third Prince pilgrimage journey. Oh, right, that would be very interesting too, and you have to give each route a different style. Indeed, if the deity is different, the main god is different, so it's naturally different. >> It’s different, and it also represents the residents who came from. those past settlements, yes, that's right. >> To be honest, I had originally prepared a lot of questions to ask the councilor , but you’ve actually already answered them for me. >> Oh, really? Is this also what you wanted to hear? >> This is really what I wanted to hear. I'm telling you, I really think there is just too much interesting stuff to talk about in New Taipei, and that’s just covering the Three-City and Coastal areas. We can definitely do city tours later on, because for places like Yonghe and Zhonghe, if you don’t actually walk into the alleys, you’ll feel like something is missing. When I.

# 永和：新北的文藝之都

was actually walking through Yonghe, I was with Yang Shuang-zi. >> No wonder. Exactly, so after Shuang-zi and I sat down at a coffee shop, they started telling me stories about Yonghe . Actually, Yonghe is extremely densely populated. If you think about its land area—I looked it up last time— it’s roughly the size of 22 Daan Forest Parks, but over 210,000 people live there. So, just imagine one Daan Forest Park packed with 10,000 people; that’s about how crowded it feels,. and that’s even before accounting for any buildings or anything else. It's just like that. It seems to be one of the most densely populated places in the world. >> So, Yonghe is truly a gathering place for talent; so many artists love to live here. From Yang San-lang in the past to Yang Shuang-zi today, really, whether they are painters or writers, everyone feels that this place has a certain aura that brings people together. That’s why I say Yonghe has a great chance of becoming New Taipei’s cultural capital. So you. might wonder, what kind of possibilities can such a crowded place have? It turns out to have infinite possibilities. I totally agree, because I grew up in Shilin. The scenery there was beautiful, and we didn't live far from where Chiang Kai-shek lived at the time. >> But later on, I went to school in Yonghe, near the Fu-Xing Trade and Arts School, yes. >> Back then, I just felt that Yonghe was very crowded, and I’d always want to escape as soon as class was over. I never expected that I’d eventually end up living nearby. I live near the. No. 4 Park now, right on the border of Yonghe and Zhonghe. >> So, what is it that you like most about Yonghe? >> I’m telling you, just like you mentioned about Yonghe—if you just drive through it, you might think it looks crowded or the streetscapes are a bit chaotic. But once you walk inside, you’ll discover many neighborhoods with planning and architecture preserved from certain past eras. I really think there is so much to discover in Yonghe. >> I think what's interesting about Yonghe is its multi-ethnic and multicultural. nature; for me, I only found out later that there were streets for other ethnic groups. >> Right, that's how it is. You later realize that while New Taipei—or Taipei County as it was—developed earlier than Taipei City, once our capital and primary city were established at this center, we naturally became a supporting player. So everyone, because the biggest opportunities are in the capital, if they couldn't afford to live in the capital, they would live right next to it. >> Yes, at first it felt a bit like a " second choice," just being close to it, but who is the closest to it? It's actually Yonghe. Exactly, it's Yonghe, so generations have come; while we have the old Yonghe residents, there are also those who came over time, whether they arrived after 1949, came up from the central or southern regions, or were students moving north. >> Right. >> Exactly, or even... >> People like me who moved here from Taipei. >> Yes, even the new immigrants today, and now people like you moving here from Taipei—it’s all there, but once everyone chooses to settle in Yonghe, they gradually feel that this place... >> It's actually because the living convenience is so good. >> Yes. >> It really is highly convenient, and after living here, you find many people who think like you; moreover, if you avoid controversial topics, you’ll find that the people here are very. willing to share their differences with one another. >> I agree. Right? So the other day, Shuangzi was telling us, and Zixun was also telling me, you can eat Tainan-style food here. >> Yes. >> And add some Sichuan chili oil to it. >> Right, this is a situation you won't find anywhere else. >> Actually, even looking at the whole world, you might not find it. >> Mm, you might not find such a dense and diverse culture in one place. >> Yes, yes, yes. And while we used the. term "new immigrants" at the beginning, they actually come from hundreds of different countries, so everyone here is very open, and it's a place that can create many new ideas; so I think Yonghe truly deserves to be a city of arts and culture—it can be the cultural capital of New Taipei. Now with Yangzi here, we’re neighbors. Exactly, I was saying that from Yang San-lang to Yang Shuang-tzu, all the literary figures chose this place, and even around this No. 4 Park, they developed a sense of Yonghe identity,. which is really a New Taipei identity. So sometimes I say that when I was a kid reading books, I was so envious that my living room was half a literary salon. >> So, this is what you were talking about regarding city identity. >> Exactly, that’s why I actually really like Yonghe. >> So, like when I blurted out "Taipei" just now, I really have been slowly building my own identity as a New Taipei citizen over these past few years. Even sometimes, for example, when I take the High Speed Rail, I get off at Banqiao. I used to go to Taipei Station, but now I always go to Banqiao. Station and the commercial districts nearby. I even watch movies there now, and I slowly feel that this is what the city I live in is really like. So, this identity is being built bit by bit. Wait, hold on. I think today there’s one question I really want to ask. As a New Taipei citizen, I’ve always been puzzled because Taiwan and Japan have such close exchanges, and we know some counties and cities establish so-called sister city relationships. >> Uh-huh. >> So I feel that New Taipei should.

# 姊妹市、城市外交與影視取景

probably pair up with Kanagawa, or maybe Chiba, or cities that correspond to Tokyo. This involves some city diplomacy, and I’m a bit confused as to why it seems like no one has made such connections in the past. Well, I think perhaps it’s not that they haven't, but rather they haven't made it clear to everyone that these connections are important, or haven't prioritized them. But I think now is exactly the right time for it. >> Right, it must be done. >> Yes, yes, yes. So I wouldn’t say nothing has been done, but I think we can do it better and make it more visible to everyone. Because, actually, my main goal is for us to be seen. >> Right. Whether it’s being seen in Taiwan as truly the biggest city, or the top city, even as a major city of 4 million people, we should have the ambition to have our own visibility internationally. That’s why I say we are the top choice for Taiwanese people to settle down, and a city that. foreigners must visit at least once in their lifetime. >> That’s great, someone finally called it out. Yes, so I think our diversity is our unique feature, and we must use our unique features to win everyone’s recognition. This is my vision and expectation for New Taipei City, and it is also the goal I am working towards. So, in this process, regarding the connections with foreign cities you just mentioned—whether through mutual cooperation, creating new things to be. seen, or using others as a reference to help us become......objects of interest , I think this is also a method. It's all about the approach. So, since you’re a Japan expert who wants to re-examine New Taipei from a Japanese perspective today, I really look forward to the opportunity on this show to share with all my friends who love visiting Japan that New Taipei actually has many wonderful attractions. Of course, I know that New Taipei’s. attractions still need a bit more effort, for instance, transportation to these spots. >> It needs to be more comfortable. Take the hiking trails we just mentioned; I feel that the transport links to get to those trails are not very convenient in New Taipei right now. After taking the MRT, you still need to transfer to a bus to reach the trailhead. After finishing a hike, going from point A to point B sometimes doesn't get you home smoothly. Just thinking, "I finally. finished the hike, do I really have to hike all the way back?" You just decide , forget it, I won't go. >> And it's not suitable to drive, because your car is parked at one point, and... right. Exactly. So these are all issues that we, as a government...... >> agency, should be able to improve, and only then can these attractions be more liked and accepted by everyone. Like the bike paths we mentioned earlier, the nodes along the way should be well-designed. And of course, this includes the city itself, which has too. many historical stories—how do we dig them up to make them interesting? For example, I should find experts like you , or even collaborate with the film and television industry; do you know how many there are? >> That’s what I wanted to say. It doesn't have to be just me. Yes, a lot of our yearning for or understanding of Japanese attractions comes from anime and movies. Exactly. >> I think more movies should be filmed in New Taipei. New Taipei has so many stories and settings, which also fits. what you said about needing to be " Instagrammable." >> For instance, even advertisements could work; it doesn't have to be limited to film and TV works. Variety shows could also work, right? You can do anything here; for instance, our coast with its three layers of sea could host the best challenge-based or stamina-testing programs, right? Sports competitions should definitely come here, like the Gongliao Triathlon or the North Coast Triathlon—they are amazing, aren't they? And take, for example, how everyone currently only thinks of Jiufen for filming "Dust in the Wind," >> or "A City of Sadness." >> And, even though Hayao Miyazaki himself denied it, everyone still thinks those are the scenes from "Spirited Away." >> You didn't know the street scenes in " Wave Makers" were filmed in Sanchong? I did. >> So, there are actually many more scenes filmed in New Taipei City, and it can be presented in diverse ways, but I hope it serves as more than just a filming location. >> I hope it can actually become the birthplace of stories. >> Mm. >> I think that would be even better; for example, our Jide Temple in Xizhi is. where "The Teenage Psychic" originated. >> Oh, really? Yes, yes, Liu Bo-jun— that’s the place where that story originated. So for us, Jide Temple eventually gained some visibility. People will come here out of curiosity and interest, and once they visit, they’ll end up loving it. The public sector can help these stories be seen; for example, I want to make New Taipei City the most film-friendly city. >> By being the friendliest place to film and encouraging everyone to come, more works will naturally be born from this city of New Taipei. That is my approach , and including what we just discussed, my ultimate dream is to let the unique characteristics of every district be seen, to have everyone appreciate the strengths of each district, and for people in every district to take pride in where they come from. "I am a Gongliao local, I am a Pingxi local, I. am a Zhonghe local, I am a Yingge local "—I want every child in every district to feel, "Yes, that’s right, I’m from Wulai." That feeling is exactly what I want, but when these 29 districts come together, >> Mm. >> I am a New Taipei citizen. >> Right. >> I am from Greater New Taipei. >> If you go to Japan in the future and tell people you are from New Taipei, they won't be surprised; they are very clear about this. >> I am from, well, bigger than Taipei, the "New" Taipei. >> A place that is bigger and more diversely developed than Taipei. >> Yes, yes, yes. Well, I feel that after our conversation today, I’m immediately inspired to make another video. Because we talked about a lot, whether it’s the unique features of each district or the comparison between New Taipei and Japan's tertiary cities, I don't think we can finish today, as I know the committee member has a busy schedule. But I promise everyone that I will turn this topic into another video.

# 結語與「新北照片」募集

to bring the vision in my head to life for everyone to see. I really feel that many things can be turned into better travel experiences, or even using tourism to get to know this city; that’s actually one of our goals and methods. Hearing this from you, I am very gratified. Why? Because I know that if one is truly serving as a leader, just dealing with civil administration issues is already. extremely busy, and then being expected to take care of tourism and city diplomacy. I almost feel bad for them. No, no, not at all. I actually think that things like travel and tourism are the best areas of expertise for this era. I’ll say it again, my goal is to achieve balanced identity for all 29 districts of New Taipei City, so in some places we rely on developing manufacturing to help them thrive and. grow better. >> But in other places we rely on tourism, and actually, for any place, I think it’s worth using tourism as a way to introduce ourselves to others, to let more people know us—is there any better way than this? So, tourism experts are the important consultants and key figures I really hope to bring together in the future. >> Sounds like we’ll have plenty of opportunities to meet in the future. That’s right, that was the plan all. along. I’m running in this election for this goal, not just to win the campaign. I hope this era allows the allocation of public resources to move in line with the pulse of the new era that I feel. I came with this hope, and I hope to call upon more people to join us. As for me, I just want to have a sense of pride and identity as a citizen, and I can use my expertise to contribute some things for it. >> Yes, and you can contribute your part, you can start by introducing Yonghe, that’s right. >> You can start by introducing Yonghe. >> Very fitting, very fitting. Wow, we actually prepared so much, and we could go on forever because, honestly, there are just so many places in New Taipei City that mirror these Japanese local lines. We are very happy to have invited Legislator Chiao, who is also a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, to our show today. I hope that shortly after this episode airs, everything we've talked about can come true. Thank. you everyone. I’m also very glad to have this opportunity today. I actually thought about asking your audience to collect photos of places that look like they’re somewhere else, but are actually in New Taipei, >> We can collect them, absolutely. Really ? Yes! So, I want to say this to the camera: to all our listeners and viewers, I’m really looking forward to it. If you know of more great places in New Taipei, could you share them with me? Even those spots where you thought, "I thought this was somewhere in Japan," or "I thought this was somewhere else," but it’s actually in New Taipei, could you share those? I. really want to know, and in the future, I will definitely make sure more people get to see these places. We can turn this into a hashtag, whether on IG or YT, that works too. Alright, thank you all for watching today. I'm Gong Tou-jian, and we'll see you next time on our podcast. >> See you next time! I hope I can come back often to share more about New Taipei with everyone.

item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

================================================

# 精華：你以為在日本，其實在新北

If we talk about New Taipei City, it's like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. That's one way to put it, it's a bit of a metaphor, yes, exactly. If you know of any other great spots in New Taipei City, could you share them with me? Even places that look like they're in Japan but are actually right here in New Taipei, could you share those too? I really want to know. Everyone wants to share the scenes they experience there with others, so being able to photograph these spots is really. important, I think. >> As I just mentioned, that's an abstract ideal, a wish of mine. # 永和：新北的文藝之都

was actually walking through Yonghe, I was with Yang Shuang-zi. >> No wonder. Exactly, so after Shuang-zi and I sat down at a coffee shop, they started telling me stories about Yonghe . Actually, Yonghe is extremely densely populated. If you think about its land area—I looked it up last time— it’s roughly the size of 22 Daan Forest Parks, but over 210,000 people live there. So, just imagine one Daan Forest Park packed with 10,000 people; that’s about how crowded it feels,. and that’s even before accounting for any buildings or anything else. It's just like that. It seems to be one of the most densely populated places in the world. >> So, Yonghe is truly a gathering place for talent; so many artists love to live here. From Yang San-lang in the past to Yang Shuang-zi today, really, whether they are painters or writers, everyone feels that this place has a certain aura that brings people together. That’s why I say Yonghe has a great chance of becoming New Taipei’s cultural capital. So you. might wonder, what kind of possibilities can such a crowded place have? It turns out to have infinite possibilities. I totally agree, because I grew up in Shilin. The scenery there was beautiful, and we didn't live far from where Chiang Kai-shek lived at the time. >> But later on, I went to school in Yonghe, near the Fu-Xing Trade and Arts School, yes. >> Back then, I just felt that Yonghe was very crowded, and I’d always want to escape as soon as class was over. I never expected that I’d eventually end up living nearby. I live near the. No. 4 Park now, right on the border of Yonghe and Zhonghe. >> So, what is it that you like most about Yonghe? >> I’m telling you, just like you mentioned about Yonghe—if you just drive through it, you might think it looks crowded or the streetscapes are a bit chaotic. But once you walk inside, you’ll discover many neighborhoods with planning and architecture preserved from certain past eras. I really think there is so much to discover in Yonghe. >> I think what's interesting about Yonghe is its multi-ethnic and multicultural. nature; for me, I only found out later that there were streets for other ethnic groups. >> Right, that's how it is. You later realize that while New Taipei—or Taipei County as it was—developed earlier than Taipei City, once our capital and primary city were established at this center, we naturally became a supporting player. So everyone, because the biggest opportunities are in the capital, if they couldn't afford to live in the capital, they would live right next to it. >> Yes, at first it felt a bit like a " second choice," just being close to it, but who is the closest to it? It's actually Yonghe. Exactly, it's Yonghe, so generations have come; while we have the old Yonghe residents, there are also those who came over time, whether they arrived after 1949, came up from the central or southern regions, or were students moving north. >> Right. >> Exactly, or even... >> People like me who moved here from Taipei. >> Yes, even the new immigrants today, and now people like you moving here from Taipei—it’s all there, but once everyone chooses to settle in Yonghe, they gradually feel that this place... >> It's actually because the living convenience is so good. >> Yes. >> It really is highly convenient, and after living here, you find many people who think like you; moreover, if you avoid controversial topics, you’ll find that the people here are very. willing to share their differences with one another. >> I agree. Right? So the other day, Shuangzi was telling us, and Zixun was also telling me, you can eat Tainan-style food here. >> Yes. >> And add some Sichuan chili oil to it. >> Right, this is a situation you won't find anywhere else. >> Actually, even looking at the whole world, you might not find it. >> Mm, you might not find such a dense and diverse culture in one place. >> Yes, yes, yes. And while we used the. term "new immigrants" at the beginning, they actually come from hundreds of different countries, so everyone here is very open, and it's a place that can create many new ideas; so I think Yonghe truly deserves to be a city of arts and culture—it can be the cultural capital of New Taipei. Now with Yangzi here, we’re neighbors. Exactly, I was saying that from Yang San-lang to Yang Shuang-tzu, all the literary figures chose this place, and even around this No. 4 Park, they developed a sense of Yonghe identity,. which is really a New Taipei identity. So sometimes I say that when I was a kid reading books, I was so envious that my living room was half a literary salon. >> So, this is what you were talking about regarding city identity. >> Exactly, that’s why I actually really like Yonghe. >> So, like when I blurted out "Taipei" just now, I really have been slowly building my own identity as a New Taipei citizen over these past few years. Even sometimes, for example, when I take the High Speed Rail, I get off at Banqiao. I used to go to Taipei Station, but now I always go to Banqiao. Station and the commercial districts nearby. I even watch movies there now, and I slowly feel that this is what the city I live in is really like. So, this identity is being built bit by bit. Wait, hold on. I think today there’s one question I really want to ask. As a New Taipei citizen, I’ve always been puzzled because Taiwan and Japan have such close exchanges, and we know some counties and cities establish so-called sister city relationships. >> Uh-huh. >> So I feel that New Taipei should.

# 姊妹市、城市外交與影視取景

probably pair up with Kanagawa, or maybe Chiba, or cities that correspond to Tokyo. This involves some city diplomacy, and I’m a bit confused as to why it seems like no one has made such connections in the past. Well, I think perhaps it’s not that they haven't, but rather they haven't made it clear to everyone that these connections are important, or haven't prioritized them. But I think now is exactly the right time for it. >> Right, it must be done. >> Yes, yes, yes. So I wouldn’t say nothing has been done, but I think we can do it better and make it more visible to everyone. Because, actually, my main goal is for us to be seen. >> Right. Whether it’s being seen in Taiwan as truly the biggest city, or the top city, even as a major city of 4 million people, we should have the ambition to have our own visibility internationally. That’s why I say we are the top choice for Taiwanese people to settle down, and a city that. foreigners must visit at least once in their lifetime. >> That’s great, someone finally called it out. Yes, so I think our diversity is our unique feature, and we must use our unique features to win everyone’s recognition. This is my vision and expectation for New Taipei City, and it is also the goal I am working towards. So, in this process, regarding the connections with foreign cities you just mentioned—whether through mutual cooperation, creating new things to be. seen, or using others as a reference to help us become......objects of interest , I think this is also a method. It's all about the approach. So, since you’re a Japan expert who wants to re-examine New Taipei from a Japanese perspective today, I really look forward to the opportunity on this show to share with all my friends who love visiting Japan that New Taipei actually has many wonderful attractions. Of course, I know that New Taipei’s. attractions still need a bit more effort, for instance, transportation to these spots. >> It needs to be more comfortable. Take the hiking trails we just mentioned; I feel that the transport links to get to those trails are not very convenient in New Taipei right now. After taking the MRT, you still need to transfer to a bus to reach the trailhead. After finishing a hike, going from point A to point B sometimes doesn't get you home smoothly. Just thinking, "I finally. finished the hike, do I really have to hike all the way back?" You just decide , forget it, I won't go. >> And it's not suitable to drive, because your car is parked at one point, and... right. Exactly. So these are all issues that we, as a government...... >> agency, should be able to improve, and only then can these attractions be more liked and accepted by everyone. Like the bike paths we mentioned earlier, the nodes along the way should be well-designed. And of course, this includes the city itself, which has too. many historical stories—how do we dig them up to make them interesting? For example, I should find experts like you , or even collaborate with the film and television industry; do you know how many there are? >> That’s what I wanted to say. It doesn't have to be just me. Yes, a lot of our yearning for or understanding of Japanese attractions comes from anime and movies. Exactly. >> I think more movies should be filmed in New Taipei. New Taipei has so many stories and settings, which also fits. what you said about needing to be " Instagrammable." >> For instance, even advertisements could work; it doesn't have to be limited to film and TV works. Variety shows could also work, right? You can do anything here; for instance, our coast with its three layers of sea could host the best challenge-based or stamina-testing programs, right? Sports competitions should definitely come here, like the Gongliao Triathlon or the North Coast Triathlon—they are amazing, aren't they? And take, for example, how everyone currently only thinks of Jiufen for filming "Dust in the Wind," >> or "A City of Sadness." >> And, even though Hayao Miyazaki himself denied it, everyone still thinks those are the scenes from "Spirited Away." >> You didn't know the street scenes in " Wave Makers" were filmed in Sanchong? I did. >> So, there are actually many more scenes filmed in New Taipei City, and it can be presented in diverse ways, but I hope it serves as more than just a filming location. >> I hope it can actually become the birthplace of stories. >> Mm. >> I think that would be even better; for example, our Jide Temple in Xizhi is. where "The Teenage Psychic" originated. >> Oh, really? Yes, yes, Liu Bo-jun— that’s the place where that story originated. So for us, Jide Temple eventually gained some visibility. People will come here out of curiosity and interest, and once they visit, they’ll end up loving it. The public sector can help these stories be seen; for example, I want to make New Taipei City the most film-friendly city. >> By being the friendliest place to film and encouraging everyone to come, more works will naturally be born from this city of New Taipei. That is my approach , and including what we just discussed, my ultimate dream is to let the unique characteristics of every district be seen, to have everyone appreciate the strengths of each district, and for people in every district to take pride in where they come from. "I am a Gongliao local, I am a Pingxi local, I. am a Zhonghe local, I am a Yingge local "—I want every child in every district to feel, "Yes, that’s right, I’m from Wulai." That feeling is exactly what I want, but when these 29 districts come together, >> Mm. >> I am a New Taipei citizen. >> Right. >> I am from Greater New Taipei. >> If you go to Japan in the future and tell people you are from New Taipei, they won't be surprised; they are very clear about this. >> I am from, well, bigger than Taipei, the "New" Taipei. >> A place that is bigger and more diversely developed than Taipei. >> Yes, yes, yes. Well, I feel that after our conversation today, I’m immediately inspired to make another video. Because we talked about a lot, whether it’s the unique features of each district or the comparison between New Taipei and Japan's tertiary cities, I don't think we can finish today, as I know the committee member has a busy schedule. But I promise everyone that I will turn this topic into another video.

# 結語與「新北照片」募集

to bring the vision in my head to life for everyone to see. I really feel that many things can be turned into better travel experiences, or even using tourism to get to know this city; that’s actually one of our goals and methods. Hearing this from you, I am very gratified. Why? Because I know that if one is truly serving as a leader, just dealing with civil administration issues is already. extremely busy, and then being expected to take care of tourism and city diplomacy. I almost feel bad for them. No, no, not at all. I actually think that things like travel and tourism are the best areas of expertise for this era. I’ll say it again, my goal is to achieve balanced identity for all 29 districts of New Taipei City, so in some places we rely on developing manufacturing to help them thrive and. grow better. >> But in other places we rely on tourism, and actually, for any place, I think it’s worth using tourism as a way to introduce ourselves to others, to let more people know us—is there any better way than this? So, tourism experts are the important consultants and key figures I really hope to bring together in the future. >> Sounds like we’ll have plenty of opportunities to meet in the future. That’s right, that was the plan all. along. I’m running in this election for this goal, not just to win the campaign. I hope this era allows the allocation of public resources to move in line with the pulse of the new era that I feel. I came with this hope, and I hope to call upon more people to join us. As for me, I just want to have a sense of pride and identity as a citizen, and I can use my expertise to contribute some things for it. >> Yes, and you can contribute your part, you can start by introducing Yonghe, that’s right. >> You can start by introducing Yonghe. >> Very fitting, very fitting. Wow, we actually prepared so much, and we could go on forever because, honestly, there are just so many places in New Taipei City that mirror these Japanese local lines. We are very happy to have invited Legislator Chiao, who is also a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, to our show today. I hope that shortly after this episode airs, everything we've talked about can come true. Thank. you everyone. I’m also very glad to have this opportunity today. I actually thought about asking your audience to collect photos of places that look like they’re somewhere else, but are actually in New Taipei, >> We can collect them, absolutely. Really ? Yes! So, I want to say this to the camera: to all our listeners and viewers, I’m really looking forward to it. If you know of more great places in New Taipei, could you share them with me? Even those spots where you thought, "I thought this was somewhere in Japan," or "I thought this was somewhere else," but it’s actually in New Taipei, could you share those? I. really want to know, and in the future, I will definitely make sure more people get to see these places. We can turn this into a hashtag, whether on IG or YT, that works too. Alright, thank you all for watching today. I'm Gong Tou-jian, and we'll see you next time on our podcast. >> See you next time! I hope I can come back often to share more about New Taipei with everyone.

=============

item.content:encoded:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

================================================

# 精華：你以為在日本，其實在新北

If we talk about New Taipei City, it's like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. That's one way to put it, it's a bit of a metaphor, yes, exactly. If you know of any other great spots in New Taipei City, could you share them with me? Even places that look like they're in Japan but are actually right here in New Taipei, could you share those too? I really want to know. Everyone wants to share the scenes they experience there with others, so being able to photograph these spots is really. important, I think. >> As I just mentioned, that's an abstract ideal, a wish of mine. But in plain terms, it just means you should be able to find what you want anywhere. Hello everyone, I’m your Chief Traveler, Kung Tung-chien. I mentioned last time that our channel would start hosting podcast-style conversations again, since we’ve done them before and are now bringing them back. We already had one guest for a conversation, and I believe many of you have already seen that video. Today, wow, I’m quite happy to discuss this topic because.

# 開場：新北是台北的 Bed Town？

last time, our conversation ended up revolving around the loneliness of modern people. >> Especially the loneliness of people in my generation—it got a bit sentimental toward the end. But today, I feel much happier because many of our viewers love traveling to Japan. That’s right, we’re going to talk about a topic related to traveling in Japan today. As you all know, over the last year or two—or rather, since the beginning of this year—I’ve been traveling the Tokaido in Japan. The Tokaido is the old road that ran from. Kyoto to Edo, and many people used this ancient route to reach Edo, which is today's Tokyo. But you’ll notice that not everyone lives in the heart of Tokyo; many people actually live in the surrounding prefectures. These are the so-called "bedroom towns" where people commute in the morning and return to sleep at night. As a resident of New Taipei City, I realized that where I live is a bit like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. This is our topic for today, and who better to. discuss it with than our guest? We’ve invited Legislative Yuan member Su Chiao-hui to join us today. Thank you, Kung Tung-chien. Hello to all the viewers, I am Otter Mom. >> When Otter Mom tells stories to children, she's "Otter Mom." >> Otter Mom is very well-known. >> Yes, yes, thank you everyone. >> So, Otter Mom also often takes everyone out on trips! >> Alright, as I mentioned earlier, while today's topic is travel-related, seeing you today made me think of something.

# 來賓登場與兩人的片場往事

that probably 99%of our audience doesn't know. We're usually so transparent, is there really something people don't know? >> We share a common experience. I heard that during the years you were studying law in the US, you worked part-time on film sets—first helping your husband with student productions in Texas—and you've even said that you were the best free labor back then. >> Oh, if you want to talk about that, are you asking if I worked as a production assistant? >> We started filming back in college, yeah, we've been filming since our. college days. Basically, it started with him as a student director and me behind the lens—wait, he was behind the lens, and I did everything else besides that, all the administrative work. So you could call me the co-producer. >> That's the truth. >> Right, you could call me an admin assistant, or a producer, anything really; it was just a two-person team, after all. OK, the reason I ask is because many people only know Janet from her days as a "travel expert," but folks, Janet was also in the film industry when she was younger. >> Really? Yes. >> I was doing production design back then , so that included building sets and everything. >> I think production design is just amazing. >> It's so exhausting. >> Production design is truly incredible. You see, they can create that entire scene from scratch. We had a famous saying back then: everything outside the camera frame is fake. Exactly, and later on, I saw how AI is so advanced now, right? A lot of things are done with green screens and computer-generated animation. >> Oh, but it's not the same. I felt that back then, production design could manage everything inside the frame,. from the color coordination to—and I'm very impressed by this—everything from the curtains and dining tables to the table runners. Even the creases in the table runners. Yes. >> Everything had to be perfectly aligned with the director's vision before the actors stepped in and we called "camera ." So, since you're so particular about the visuals, I have a sudden question: when you go to a place now, is your first thought whether it's a good spot to film? Yes.

# 用拍片的眼光看景點：一定要有打卡點

>> Honestly, yes. I truly believe that where we've been leaves a mark, and no experience is ever wasted. I really enjoy having studied law; I feel that my ability to analyze, break down, and synthesize logic and situations has been incredibly helpful, making me much more efficient at handling things now and easier to grasp the crux of an issue. And I feel that in this realm of filming and producing movies, I've also learned a great deal from every single role in the process, since making a. movie is a collaborative effort. For instance, whenever I see a scene now, I find myself thinking about which spot or which angle is the one I want most —if I could only take one photo. >> What is the specific shot that could capture the scene before me and turn it into a story to tell others? >> Or, what is the final image I want to leave behind from this press conference ? >> This idea of deciding what final image I want to capture in a place has almost. become a standard procedure for me, or perhaps, is it >> a kind of pursuit? >> Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. So, I feel that when I look at a scenic spot now, if I ever have the chance to, say, develop a tourism industry, I would really want to create that one specific image that stays in people's hearts. I believe that when there's an image that sticks with visitors, they'll come back a second, third, or fourth time, and bring even more people with them. >> Absolutely, and I have to add one more. point. Because nowadays, everyone has social media—whether it's Instagram, or like me, doing YouTube—everyone wants to share the image of where they are with others, so being able to photograph a spot is really important. >> What I said earlier was an abstract ideal, my wish, but in plain terms, it just means that every place needs a landmark photo spot that makes people want to come back. >> Whether it's natural or man-made, nowadays, it's all about that photo op. It's a must! Which leads us to our topic today: it's essentially a conversation between two New Taipei City residents. >> But in fact, many New Taipei residents are likely just like us; I was born in Yilan, moved to Taipei with my grandfather, and then my father moved us to New Taipei. Many New Taipei residents weren't necessarily born here , but it's precisely because of this that people from all different counties.

# 從東海道宿場談到「衛星變繁星」

and cities live here. >> Exactly. >> We finally, or I should say, we eventually came to treat this place as a—that’s wonderful. Hearing you say that makes us very happy. Yes. >> Really, really, really. Maybe people moved here at first because the housing prices over there were too high to afford, but after moving, they really started to treat this place as their home. Returning to what I mentioned earlier, I’m currently walking the Tokaido. People might still have the impression of the Tokaido as a place in period dramas where feudal lords are. carried in palanquins, but having reached the final stretch, I’ve found that what I’ve seen the most along the way are post stations. These so-called post stations were where people used to stay; after walking for a stretch, they needed a place to stop for the night, so these stations naturally formed settlements. >> Those post stations have now become satellite cities around Tokyo, gradually developing from those original settlements. When Japan began building its railways, the first line. ran from Shimbashi to Yokohama, and then it extended along what is known as the Tokaido, connecting all these post stations. If you look at this narrative , it’s actually exactly the same in Taiwan. >> Exactly the same. >> Exactly the same; our historical development is almost identical. >> Yes, and the railway line, what used to be the main thoroughfare, is now the railway line, and many people from the south traveled up along it. Now, what I want to say is... >> Around us now, it has actually developed around Taipei into... >> How many districts are there in total? 29 districts. In New Taipei City? 29 districts, yes. >> New Taipei City now has 29 districts. So these are all issues that we, as a government...... >> agency, should be able to improve, and only then can these attractions be more liked and accepted by everyone. Like the bike paths we mentioned earlier, the nodes along the way should be well-designed. And of course, this includes the city itself, which has too. many historical stories—how do we dig them up to make them interesting? For example, I should find experts like you , or even collaborate with the film and television industry; do you know how many there are? >> That’s what I wanted to say. It doesn't have to be just me. Yes, a lot of our yearning for or understanding of Japanese attractions comes from anime and movies. Exactly. >> I think more movies should be filmed in New Taipei. New Taipei has so many stories and settings, which also fits. what you said about needing to be " Instagrammable." >> For instance, even advertisements could work; it doesn't have to be limited to film and TV works. Variety shows could also work, right? You can do anything here; for instance, our coast with its three layers of sea could host the best challenge-based or stamina-testing programs, right? Sports competitions should definitely come here, like the Gongliao Triathlon or the North Coast Triathlon—they are amazing, aren't they? And take, for example, how everyone currently only thinks of Jiufen for filming "Dust in the Wind," >> or "A City of Sadness." >> And, even though Hayao Miyazaki himself denied it, everyone still thinks those are the scenes from "Spirited Away." >> You didn't know the street scenes in " Wave Makers" were filmed in Sanchong? I did. >> So, there are actually many more scenes filmed in New Taipei City, and it can be presented in diverse ways, but I hope it serves as more than just a filming location. >> I hope it can actually become the birthplace of stories. >> Mm. >> I think that would be even better; for example, our Jide Temple in Xizhi is. where "The Teenage Psychic" originated. >> Oh, really? Yes, yes, Liu Bo-jun— that’s the place where that story originated. So for us, Jide Temple eventually gained some visibility. People will come here out of curiosity and interest, and once they visit, they’ll end up loving it. The public sector can help these stories be seen; for example, I want to make New Taipei City the most film-friendly city. >> By being the friendliest place to film and encouraging everyone to come, more works will naturally be born from this city of New Taipei. That is my approach , and including what we just discussed, my ultimate dream is to let the unique characteristics of every district be seen, to have everyone appreciate the strengths of each district, and for people in every district to take pride in where they come from. "I am a Gongliao local, I am a Pingxi local, I. am a Zhonghe local, I am a Yingge local "—I want every child in every district to feel, "Yes, that’s right, I’m from Wulai." That feeling is exactly what I want, but when these 29 districts come together, >> Mm. >> I am a New Taipei citizen. >> Right. >> I am from Greater New Taipei. >> If you go to Japan in the future and tell people you are from New Taipei, they won't be surprised; they are very clear about this. >> I am from, well, bigger than Taipei, the "New" Taipei. >> A place that is bigger and more diversely developed than Taipei. >> Yes, yes, yes. Well, I feel that after our conversation today, I’m immediately inspired to make another video. Because we talked about a lot, whether it’s the unique features of each district or the comparison between New Taipei and Japan's tertiary cities, I don't think we can finish today, as I know the committee member has a busy schedule. But I promise everyone that I will turn this topic into another video.

# 結語與「新北照片」募集

to bring the vision in my head to life for everyone to see. I really feel that many things can be turned into better travel experiences, or even using tourism to get to know this city; that’s actually one of our goals and methods. Hearing this from you, I am very gratified. Why? Because I know that if one is truly serving as a leader, just dealing with civil administration issues is already. extremely busy, and then being expected to take care of tourism and city diplomacy. I almost feel bad for them. No, no, not at all. I actually think that things like travel and tourism are the best areas of expertise for this era. I’ll say it again, my goal is to achieve balanced identity for all 29 districts of New Taipei City, so in some places we rely on developing manufacturing to help them thrive and. grow better. >> But in other places we rely on tourism, and actually, for any place, I think it’s worth using tourism as a way to introduce ourselves to others, to let more people know us—is there any better way than this? So, tourism experts are the important consultants and key figures I really hope to bring together in the future. >> Sounds like we’ll have plenty of opportunities to meet in the future. That’s right, that was the plan all. along. I’m running in this election for this goal, not just to win the campaign. I hope this era allows the allocation of public resources to move in line with the pulse of the new era that I feel. I came with this hope, and I hope to call upon more people to join us. As for me, I just want to have a sense of pride and identity as a citizen, and I can use my expertise to contribute some things for it. >> Yes, and you can contribute your part, you can start by introducing Yonghe, that’s right. >> You can start by introducing Yonghe. >> Very fitting, very fitting. Wow, we actually prepared so much, and we could go on forever because, honestly, there are just so many places in New Taipei City that mirror these Japanese local lines. We are very happy to have invited Legislator Chiao, who is also a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, to our show today. I hope that shortly after this episode airs, everything we've talked about can come true. Thank. you everyone. I’m also very glad to have this opportunity today. I actually thought about asking your audience to collect photos of places that look like they’re somewhere else, but are actually in New Taipei, >> We can collect them, absolutely. Really ? Yes! So, I want to say this to the camera: to all our listeners and viewers, I’m really looking forward to it. If you know of more great places in New Taipei, could you share them with me? Even those spots where you thought, "I thought this was somewhere in Japan," or "I thought this was somewhere else," but it’s actually in New Taipei, could you share those? I. really want to know, and in the future, I will definitely make sure more people get to see these places. We can turn this into a hashtag, whether on IG or YT, that works too. Alright, thank you all for watching today. I'm Gong Tou-jian, and we'll see you next time on our podcast. >> See you next time! I hope I can come back often to share more about New Taipei with everyone.
